The standard length of Black cardinalfish (Epigonus telescopus) reaches an ultimate maximum of 75 centimetres [Li = 75 centimetres], a size that places it among the larger members of the Epigonidae. This species inhabits the mesopelagic to bathypelagic zones of the southern oceans, where it is frequently captured at depths exceeding 300 metres. The deepwater environment imposes strong constraints on growth and metabolism, with ambient water temperatures typically remaining around 8.9 °C [T = 8.9 °C] throughout the year. Under these stable thermal conditions, individuals have been documented to live for a maximum of 38,325 days [am = 38,325 days], or roughly 105 years, a longevity that is remarkable among teleosts and suggests a life history strategy oriented toward slow, sustained investment at a temperature of 8.9 °C [T = 8.9 °C]. The extreme lifespan likely reflects low metabolic demands at depth coupled with minimal predation pressure on adult fish. This extended existence allows for considerable accumulation of somatic tissue over time.

Puberty in Epigonus telescopus, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, is attained at a standard length of 56 centimetres [Lp = 56 centimetres]. At this size, individuals reach a wet weight at puberty of approximately 3,160 grams [Wwp = approximately 3,160 grams], a substantial body mass consistent with the energetic requirements of deepwater reproduction. The development of mature gonads in this species is a protracted process, likely spanning several years given the cold temperatures of its habitat. The standard length at puberty represents approximately 75 percent of the ultimate standard length, a proportion that accords with late-maturing deep-sea fishes. This delayed maturity is thought to reflect a bet-hedging strategy, whereby individuals invest heavily in somatic growth before committing to the considerable energetic costs associated with reproduction. The body mass at this stage is estimated using length-weight relationships calibrated for the species.

At birth, the wet weight of a newly emerged yolk-sac larva is only 0.000113 grams [Wwb = 0.000113 grams], an extremely diminutive mass that underscores the planktonic start to life in this species. This value is derived from an assumed egg diameter of 0.6 millimetres, a measurement based on the congeneric species Epigonus affinis, for which the mean egg size has been reliably documented. The small larval size indicates that the early life stages are highly vulnerable to starvation and predation, a common pattern among teleosts that produce large numbers of small offspring. The yolk reserves must sustain the larva through the lecithotrophic phase until the mouth opens and exogenous feeding begins. The duration of this yolk-dependent period remains poorly characterized for this species, but by analogy with other deepwater cardinalfishes, it likely occupies several weeks at 8.9 °C [T = 8.9 °C], the ambient temperature of its environment.

Field surveys and otolith-based growth reconstructions indicate that the ultimate wet weight attained by adult Black cardinalfish reaches 7,770 grams [Wwi = 7,770 grams], a mass that corresponds to the upper bound of the species' size distribution. This maximum weight is achieved through the cumulative growth achieved over the remarkably long lifespan, with asymptotic size approached only in the largest and oldest individuals. The length-weight relationship used to derive this value follows the allometric equation W = 0.01950 × L^2.98, which has been validated for the species from trawl samples across the southern Atlantic and Indian Oceans. The exponent of 2.98 indicates near-isometric scaling, whereby body mass increases in close proportion to the cube of length. Regular trawl surveys in the waters around New Zealand and the Southern Ocean have consistently yielded specimens approaching this ultimate weight, confirming that the species attains a remarkably large body size for a deep-sea planktivore.

Under the stable thermal regime of 8.9 °C [T = 8.9 °C] characteristic of its deepwater habitat, Epigonus telescopus maintains a reproductive rate that is notably low for a teleost of its size. Available field data suggest that each sexually mature female produces approximately 960 eggs per day on average throughout the spawning season, a figure that corresponds to roughly 350,400 eggs per year when integrated across the approximately 365-day annual cycle. This daily egg production rate is achieved through the continuous release of small batches over an extended spawning period that may last for many months. The reproductive strategy appears to be one of moderate fecundity offset by very high parental investment in each egg, which is relatively large for a deepwater species. The comparatively low daily output is consistent across individuals when they are under the stable thermal conditions of their environment, which minimizes metabolic variation.
